newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU gives Belgrade conditional trade deal.
newsitem.headline: EU gives Belgrade conditional trade deal.

text.p: The European Union granted special trade privileges to rump Yugoslavia on Tuesday but warned that lack of democratic progress or backtracking from the Dayton peace agreement would lead to their withdrawal.

Foreign ministers from the 15-nation bloc said in a statement that the move was a recognition of various moves taken by Belgrade, including allowing opposition parties to debate on television and agreeing to changes in its media laws.

The trade benefits -- which include offering duty-free access and eliminating quantitative restrictions on industrial products -- were also needed to help the country's struggling economy, the statement said.
But the deal was for 1997 only and was conditional both on further democratic reforms and on Belgrade's implementation of its commitments to the Bosnian peace accord.
Officials in Belgrade welcomed the EU move.

"This is really great news, even though it was expected. It is a recognition of positive changes in Yugoslavia by the EU ministers and we see their decision as support to continue with reforms," Deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic told Reuters.
The government of President Slobodan Milosevic is struggling to revive its stagnant economy after years of sanctions imposed by the international community.

The United Nations slapped a trade embargo on Belgrade in 1992 for its role in the Bosnian war. It was lifted last October, but a so-called "outer wall" was left in place while Serbia's behaviour was monitored, particularly in the mostly Albanian province of Kosovo.
The EU said it expected the Milosevic government to begin talks with the opposition in Belgrade, to make more improvements to its media laws, and to reform its electoral law and judicial system.
"In the absence of progress...towards meeting these criteria the decision on granting autonomous trade preferences will be reviewed," the statement said.
It also said it expected Belgrade to make "susbtantial progress" on the issue of Kosovo.
Kosovo Albanian leader Ibrahim Rugova appealed to the European Union on Monday not to grant economic and trade preferentials to Yugoslavia before the question of the province was resolved.
He said in a letter to Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo that the overall situation in Kosovo was "repressive, grave and dangerous" due to the Serbian regime's practices.
